prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level and opened a regime of many-body precision physics.

statement.case_for: I move my preferred configuration from B024 to B031. In round 1 I wrote that if the reservations about twisted bilayer graphene carried the room, the lattice clock would be the safer choice, and after reading the full exchange I think they do carry it, on grounds I share as a condensed-matter theorist. On the chair's question about distinctness: the decisive step is not a better laser or a better counting of cycles, which is what the 2005 comb prize recognised, nor control of a single ion, which is the 2012 prize. It is the realisation that the light shift of a trapping lattice can be made to cancel for the clock transition at a magic wavelength, so that of order 10^4 to 10^6 neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated at once. That changes the statistical limit on stability by orders of magnitude, and it is what allowed independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) to agree at the 10^-18 level, which is exactly the kind of cross-checked, reproducible result I trust. It has also produced new physics, not only a better number: spin-exchange and many-body effects inside the clock, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, and bounds on varying constants. Theory and experiment are tied together throughout, since the systematic budget (blackbody shift, higher-order lattice shifts, collisions) is a controlled calculation checked against measurement. A citation that names magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms in a lattice states the distinct step and avoids reading as a second frequency-comb prize. The two names map onto the two parts of the credit that five members describe identically: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, Ye for the accuracy, stability and many-body programme.
statement.case_against: Three reservations remain and I do not dismiss them. First, novelty: a sceptic can still read the lattice clock as a very well executed refinement of optical frequency standards recognised in 2005 and 2012, and the committee should decide that explicitly and not by default. Second, priority: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley and others made decisive early or record demonstrations, and I cannot settle from memory how much of the first operating clock belongs to Katori's group alone; the two-name limit may leave out real contributors. Third, timing: the redefinition of the second has not taken place, so some of the strongest applications are prospective. I also note honestly that B024 is, in my own judgement, the scientifically most novel case on the list, and moving away from it is a judgement about maturity and attribution (the first experimental author of the 2018 papers is outside any three-person set), not a change in my view of the physics.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B024 first with Bistritzer included, wants the citation built around flat bands and correlated states and not a pairing mechanism, and disagrees with my optimistic reading of timing.
responses.response: I accept your point on the citation and I am glad the Bistritzer attribution argument held. On timing I have moved toward your caution, not away from it: you apply a standard of understood mechanism to other candidates, and by that standard I cannot ask the room to carry a prize whose headline superconducting phase is not understood and whose lead experimental credit cannot be represented. I would be glad to see B024 recognised in a later year, with the same three names and a flat-band and correlated-states citation, once there is another few years of independent replication in several moire platforms. For this year I invite you to say whether B031 is acceptable to you as second choice, which is the chair's question to you, and whether novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 is your only objection. My answer on novelty is the magic-wavelength lattice, as above.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B031 first on maturity, cross-checked independent confirmation and clean attribution, and holds B024 as possibly premature given an unsettled pairing mechanism.
responses.response: In round 1 I disagreed that an open pairing mechanism made the discovery premature, and I still think the cuprate analogy is fair. But you ask a more practical question, and the answer for this year is the one you gave: the clock has agreement among independent laboratories at 10^-18, and that is a firmer base. I also answer the question I put to you, how decisive the lattice step is: it is the cancellation of the light shift in the lattice, which lets a neutral-atom ensemble reach stability that ion clocks cannot. I would ask you and Pearce to include 'magic wavelength' in the citation text for that reason.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the early strontium lattice priority of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates is settled, and whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I cannot settle the priority question from memory either, and I agree it should be checked before the final ballot. My working position is that the proposal of the magic wavelength and the first operating lattice clock are Katori's, and that the accuracy and many-body programme is Ye's, which is the division you also describe. If the record shows that a third laboratory made a decision step that is not covered by the proposal or the first demonstration, I would want that discussed rather than silently dropped, even though the three-person limit would then force a choice. On waiting for the redefinition, I do not think a formal metrology decision is a criterion of scientific discovery. The agreement of independent clocks at the 10^-18 level already is the discovery.

responses.point: Johansson says the B024 experimental credit may include Cao and others outside the three names, and that the clock is the discovery-first, instrument-second case with unusually clean attribution.
responses.response: Our views have converged. I said the Cao point is a limit of the three-laureate rule, and you correctly treat that limit as practical, since it cannot be fixed by the committee without dropping a theorist. I agree with your discovery-first, instrument-second reading of B031, which also answers Olsson's category question: it comes with a fundamental-physics return in gravitational redshift tests and constants, which is why I would rank it above B009 as an instrument. I also note that you mention the open question of whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, and I would not.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B005 first, argues that the Higgs observation tested a precise quantitative prediction, and says he would re-rank B024 upward if the superconducting state were better understood.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation is the cleaner test of a precise prediction, and I do not dispute its science; I defer to you and Pearce on particle physics. My difficulty is the same as the chair's: I cannot propose a rule that gives a stable three-name allocation among the founding leaders and 2012 spokespeople of ATLAS and CMS, and I do not want the committee to choose three names arbitrarily. If you or Pearce can state a rule that the room would accept, I would listen, but absent that I cannot make B005 a preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley, which I recall only from memory, supports limiting the credit to Katori and Ye.
Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a step distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the committee will find a defensible way to weigh B024 against clock maturity in a later cycle, since I still regard moire quantum matter as a strong future candidate.
How the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits, which I chaired, should weigh on the timing of B016; I do not think it bears on B031.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known collaboration with Katori or Ye, nor with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and no conflict for B031 or B024. I chaired the 2025 committee, which bears on the timing of B016 but is not a personal connection requiring recusal. My theory work supports experiments at MAX IV and ESS and is not related to optical clocks.
